title: Validate remediation SLA matrix vs Dedicated/Private customer commitments (incl. region-wide + cloud outage edge cases)
creator: Rachel Kim
project: Reliability Program: Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping
description:
## Context
SRE is rolling out a standardized incident taxonomy + ownership mapping, with remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix) enforced via incident-bot and breach alerting (ENG-4829).

Before enforcement, we need to validate that the proposed remediation SLAs for **Dedicated** and **Private** align with:
- customer-facing commitments (MSA/order forms + Dedicated/Private reliability addenda)
- how Support/CS communicates “next update” and “mitigation/fix ETA” today
- realistic operational constraints (fleet capacity, region failover realities)

This ticket is specifically to close gaps and document edge-case carve-outs so we don’t ship a policy that conflicts with contract language or sets unachievable expectations.

## Goals / deliverables
1) Produce a written confirmation (one-pager) that the remediation SLA matrix used by tooling is aligned with Dedicated/Private commitments.
2) Explicitly document carve-outs and handling rules for:
   - region-wide events
   - cloud provider outages / upstream incidents
   - customer-caused incidents (e.g., misconfiguration, abusive traffic patterns)
   - force majeure
   - multi-cause incidents (capacity + routing, control plane + auth)
3) Decide what becomes:
   - a strict SLA timer (breach alerting)
   - a target / internal SLO (tracked, but not considered a “breach” for customer commitments)
4) Provide inputs to SRE + Tooling so implementation is consistent (ENG-4829, incident-bot gating).

## Inputs / references
- Confluence: incident taxonomy + remediation SLA matrix
  - sources/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-ownership-mapping-and-remediation-sla-matrix.json
- Support/CS comms usage of taxonomy
  - sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook/using-incident-taxonomy-for-customer-comms.json
- Tooling: remediation SLA timers + breach alerting
  - ENG-4829

## Key questions to resolve
### A) What exactly are we promising?
We need to be careful about terminology. Some customers interpret “SLA” as contractual service credits, while internally we also use “SLA” to mean operational commitments.
- Confirm: for Dedicated/Private, do we describe remediation times as:
  - contractual (credit-bearing) OR
  - operational commitments (documented + tracked, but not credit-bearing)
- Confirm: which severities apply to contractual commitments (Sev0/Sev1 only?)

### B) Start/stop and pause rules (timer semantics)
Align a clear, auditable definition across tiers.
- Start time: when incident is declared in incident-bot (preferred) vs when customer first impacted vs when page fired.
- Pause conditions:
  - declared upstream cloud provider outage (AWS/GCP incident) that is the dominant cause
  - customer-caused / customer-controlled blast radius (e.g., invalid routing policy pushed by customer in Private)
  - force majeure
- Resume conditions: when there is actionable work under Redwood control.

### C) Region-wide events / cloud provider outages
Edge case we have to nail:
- If the primary mitigation is “fail over to another region,” is that considered mitigation complete even if capacity is degraded (e.g., higher latency / lower throughput)?
- For Dedicated: if customer is pinned to a region by contract or data residency, what is the expected mitigation path?
- For Private: if the customer’s network path (DNS/TLS) is the cause, do we treat it as an incident with a remediation SLA or as support/engagement guidance only?

### D) Multi-cause incidents and attribution
Operationally we will choose one **primary incident_type**, with contributing factors noted. For remediation SLAs:
- Confirm which category sets the timer (primary type only)
- Confirm whether certain types always supersede others for contractual commitments (e.g., control plane outage vs latency regression)

## Proposed alignment (draft; validate against commitments)
This is not attempting to rewrite SRE’s matrix; it’s the set of guardrails we need for Dedicated/Private.

1) **Dedicated**
- Sev0/Sev1 remediation targets should be treated as externally meaningful commitments (CS will communicate against them).
- If there is a declared upstream cloud provider outage affecting the contracted region:
  - timer may pause for “time-to-fix,” but we still commit to an update cadence and reasonable mitigations under our control (e.g., routing policy overrides, traffic shaping, failover where allowed).
- Capacity shortage incidents:
  - Mitigation can be “throttle + explicit degradation mode + controlled fallback” if it restores availability within the customer’s documented behavior expectations.

2) **Private (VPC/on-prem)**
- Remediation SLAs should distinguish between:
  - Redwood-controlled components (control plane, agent, upgrade tooling)
  - customer-controlled networking/environment (DNS, TLS, firewall, egress)
- For customer-controlled causes, we should track as an incident for learning, but not count as an SLA breach.

3) **Update cadence vs mitigation vs fix**
Even in edge cases where fix SLA is paused, Dedicated/Private should still have:
- a “time-to-first-update” expectation (comms)
- a “time-to-mitigation under Redwood control” expectation (e.g., rollback, traffic shift)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Lauren + Vivek sign off on Dedicated + Private carve-outs and timer semantics.
- [ ] SRE (Rafael) confirms that the policy language can be implemented in ENG-4829 without manual exceptions every time.
- [ ] CS/Support (Dev Patel) confirms comms language is consistent with escalation playbook.
- [ ] Final notes posted back into Confluence remediation SLA matrix page (or linked addendum) and referenced in incident classification policy.

## Open items / risks
- Risk: shipping breach alerting before policy is clear will create “false breaches,” desensitizing on-call and confusing CS.
- Risk: “cloud outage” carve-out can become an escape hatch unless we define evidence required (link to provider status + internal indicators).
- Risk: Dedicated commitments vary by contract; we need a minimum common policy + documented overrides.

## Next steps
1) Pull current Dedicated/Private commitment language (Product Ops) and summarize the relevant clauses in a shareable snippet.
2) 30-min review with SRE + Support + Dedicated PM.
3) Finalize timer semantics + carve-out rules and hand back to ENG-4829 implementation.
comments: 2025-12-11 — Lauren Bishop: Pulled a sample of 6 Dedicated order forms. Most use availability credits; remediation times are referenced as “operational targets” in the reliability addendum. Need to confirm we don’t label these as credit-bearing SLAs in tooling/UI.

2025-12-16 — Vivek Kulkarni: For Private, we must treat customer networking issues (DNS/TLS/firewall) as non-breach unless Redwood-provided upgrade tooling introduced the config change. Propose a required field in incident-bot: customer_caused=true|false (or a carve-out reason).

2026-01-06 — Dev Patel: CS wants a separate concept of “update cadence” even when upstream outage pauses fix timer. Customers primarily escalate when they don’t get updates, not when fix takes longer due to AWS/GCP events.

2026-01-14 — Rafael Mendes: From implementation standpoint, we can support (a) pause_reason enum (cloud_outage, customer_caused, force_majeure) and (b) require evidence link in the incident timeline. But we should keep pause reasons low-cardinality.

2026-01-20 — Rachel Kim: Proposed wording for Confluence addendum: remediation SLA timers are operational commitments; contractual credits remain governed by the MSA and availability SLA. Waiting on Dedicated PM signoff re: whether any customers have explicit mitigation/fix time guarantees.

2026-02-02 — Lauren Bishop: Dedicated stakeholder review complete. We’re aligned on pausing fix timer for verified cloud provider incidents, but mitigation timer should still run for actions under our control (routing overrides, rollback). Request SRE confirm matrix can represent split semantics cleanly.
